planting.note: Fall-sow onto bare mineral soil so seed gets natural winter chilling and surface light exposure, or set out small container plugs in early spring; this shrub resprouts from root crowns after fire or mowing, unlike big sagebrush.

directions: Threetip sagebrush forms dense, three-lobed-leaved colonies across the Snake River Plain, Palouse hills, and Great Basin benchlands, distinguished from big sagebrush by its shorter stature and tendency to resprout vigorously from the root crown after disturbance. Narrow, silvery, deeply three-cleft leaves release a sharp sage scent and persist through winter, with small flower heads opening on upright spikes from late summer into fall. It needs lean, well-drained soil and essentially no irrigation once established, and like other sagebrushes it declines quickly in rich or heavily watered garden beds. Use it where fire or periodic cutting is part of the management plan, since it tolerates both far better than non-resprouting sagebrush species.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center (Aberdeen, Idaho) Plant Guide
USDA Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station
University of Idaho Extension

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed shallowly in fall onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in shallow, rocky-to-clay soil, since seed needs surface light and winter chilling to germinate and buried seed fails.

directions: Low sagebrush is a diminutive, slow-growing dwarf shrub that carpets shallow, rocky, clay-heavy ridgetops and scabland flats across the Great Basin and Snake River Plain where taller sagebrush species cannot root deeply. Its tiny, wedge-shaped silver leaves form a dense, low mat rarely over a foot tall, making it valuable winter forage and cover for sage grouse and pygmy rabbits. It demands extremely lean, shallow, rocky soil in full sun and resents any amendment, deep soil, or regular watering, all of which favor weedy competitors over its naturally slow growth. Collect or source seed carefully since its low stature makes wild seed collection difficult and commercial supply limited.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide (ARAR8)
Great Basin Native Plant Project
Calscape / California Native Plant Society

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into deep, moisture-retentive soil, since seed from the colder, drier end of its range needs roughly four weeks of cold-moist stratification and the stout taproot transplants poorly after the first year.

directions: Mule's ears is one of the most conspicuous spring wildflowers of the sagebrush-steppe and bunchgrass prairies spanning the Snake River Plain, Palouse, and Great Basin, named for its large, glossy, lance-shaped basal leaves. Bright yellow, daisy-like blooms several inches across open atop coarse stems in late spring, often carpeting entire hillsides alongside arrowleaf balsamroot. It favors deep, seasonally moist clay or loam soils in sagebrush flats and mountain meadows rather than the leanest, rockiest ground, and once its deep taproot is established it needs no summer water. Give it room, since large stands can dominate a planting the way they dominate their native range.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
Washington Native Plant Society
University of Washington ESRM Native Plant Propagation Protocol Database

planting.note: Dormant-seed in fall onto a firm, weed-free bed so the fibrous, awned seed experiences winter freeze-thaw cycles; germination under cultivation is naturally slow and uneven, and most supply comes as 'source-identified' restoration seed rather than retail nursery stock.

directions: Thurber's needlegrass is a fine-leaved, cool-season bunchgrass that fills the interspaces between sagebrush plants across the Snake River Plain and Great Basin, named for its long, twisted, bristle-like awns that catch morning dew and glint silver in the wind. It cures to a pale straw color by midsummer and relies entirely on winter and spring moisture, going fully dormant through the dry season. Grow it in lean, well-drained soil with no summer irrigation as a textural companion grass between sagebrush and steppe wildflowers rather than a lawn substitute. Because wildland seed production is erratic, source seed from a restoration seed supplier serving the Intermountain West rather than general retail nurseries.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide (ACTH7)
Utah State University Extension Rangeplants
USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat before fall sowing directly into lean, well-drained soil, since the deep taproot resents transplanting and untreated seed can remain dormant for a full season.

directions: Basalt milkvetch is an upright, silvery-leaved legume scattered through sagebrush steppe and basalt-scabland openings of the Snake River Plain and Great Basin, taller and more erect than most of its milkvetch relatives. Cream to pale lilac pea-like flowers cluster along the stems in late spring and are heavily worked by native bees, making it one of the few native legumes widely used in pollinator-focused restoration seedings. As a nitrogen-fixer it needs no fertility input and performs best in lean, gravelly soil with no summer water. Because wildland seed crops are unpredictable, most garden supply comes from cultivated restoration seed growers rather than general nurseries.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide (basalt milkvetch)
USDA Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station
Utah State University

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, dry, rocky soil so the hard nutlets cold-stratify naturally over winter, since the woody taproot forms quickly and makes bare-root transplanting unreliable after the first season.

directions: Western stoneseed sends up a cluster of leafy stems from a stout, woody taproot in sagebrush steppe and dry open ground across the Snake River Plain and Palouse country, with small, pale yellow to greenish-white tubular flowers tucked among the upper leaves in early to mid spring. The hard, bony seed nutlets that follow were historically gathered and strung as beads, and the deep red-dyeing root was once a notable dye source for regional tribes. It thrives in nutrient-poor, rocky, or sandy soils with excellent drainage and needs no supplemental water once its taproot is established, though young plants benefit from staying undisturbed through their first couple of seasons. Site it in a lean rock garden or dry steppe planting rather than enriched beds, which cause weak, leggy growth.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
Burke Museum Herbarium, University of Washington
Washington Native Plant Society

planting.note: Sow in fall so seed experiences natural winter chilling, into open, well-drained soil in full sun; plants emerge and bloom very early in spring and go dormant by summer, so site them where later-emerging neighbors can fill the gap.

directions: Oblongleaf bluebells push up thick, branching stems from a woody caudex among sagebrush and bunchgrasses across the Snake River Plain and Intermountain foothills, one of the earliest wildflowers to bloom as snow recedes. Clusters of nodding, bell-shaped flowers open blue with a pink-tinted bud stage, held above oval-to-lance leaves that rarely exceed a foot in height. Unlike its moist-woodland relatives, this is a true dryland bluebell, thriving in open, well-drained slopes with no summer irrigation and going summer-dormant soon after bloom. Pair it with later-season steppe wildflowers so the garden has continued interest once its above-ground growth dies back.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
Burke Museum Herbarium, University of Washington
PNW Flowers (University of Washington)

planting.note: Sow seed directly where it is to grow in fall, since the thick carrot-like taproot resents disturbance; seed requires an extended cold-moist winter chill and plants commonly take several years to reach flowering size.

directions: Bigseed biscuitroot sprawls low over gravelly scabland and dry bunchgrass-steppe ground across the Snake River Plain and Columbia Basin, with gray-green, finely divided, hairy foliage and flattened umbels of white to purplish or yellowish flowers in early spring. It was among the most important root-food plants for Columbia Plateau and Great Basin tribes, dug and dried into cakes after its edible taproot was peeled and cooked. Grow it in lean, rocky, or sandy soil with sharp drainage and no summer water, siting seed directly in its permanent spot since the taproot does not transplant. Expect a slow start: plants often take a few years from seed before they flower reliably.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
Idaho Department of Fish and Game Species Profile
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center
